query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a pack-cementation silicide surface treatment to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will form a thin, adherent silicide layer that significantly limits oxygen ingress during high‐temperature exposure, thereby preventing pesting without degrading its inherent room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxidation resistance.
generation.intervention: Pack-cementation-based silicide treatment performed at approximately 1000 °C for several hours to deposit a controlled silicide layer (target thickness ~10–50 µm) on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at temperatures between 800 °C and 1000 °C for at least 5 hours. Mechanical performance to be evaluated under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous silicide scale formed on the surface that acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen.
generation.mechanism: The silicide layer reduces oxygen diffusion into the bulk material by functioning as a protective barrier, thereby mitigating the pesting effect. Because the treatment is confined to the surface, the bulk microstructure and its advantageous mechanical properties remain essentially unchanged.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated specimens will exhibit significantly lower oxidation rates (e.g., reduced mass gain and scale spallation) during high-temperature exposure compared to untreated samples, while retaining similar tensile ductility and yield strength at both room temperature and 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which suffers from oxidation-induced degradation (pesting) under high-temperature air exposure for durations of ≥5 hours, thus limiting its practical use despite good mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under air exposures at 800–1000 °C for durations of 5 hours or more. The intervention must provide a silicide layer of controlled thickness (approximately 10–50 µm) to avoid adverse embrittlement of the near-surface region during subsequent mechanical loading.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of the silicide layer formation, its long-term adhesion under cyclic thermal/mechanical loads, and any potential subtle changes in fatigue or fracture behavior remain to be quantitatively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set receives the pack-cementation silicide treatment (applied at ~1000 °C for 3–5 hours) and the other set remains untreated. Expose both sets to air at a controlled temperature (e.g., 900 °C) for 5 hours. Subsequently, perform detailed surface characterization (using SEM/EDS or XRD) to assess oxide and silicide scale formation and measure mass gain. Finally, conduct tensile testing at room temperature and 1000 °C (under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) on both sets to evaluate any differences in mechanical performance.
measurements: Mass change (mg/cm²) to assess oxidation kinetics
Microstructural analysis of the surface scale (thickness, continuity, phase composition)
Room-temperature and high-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength
Fractography to detect signs of embrittlement or interfacial failures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples show oxidation characteristics (e.g., mass gain, scale spallation or non-uniform silicide formation) that are indistinguishable from the untreated samples, or if their mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) are significantly degraded relative to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. decision.trend: Studies on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr have primarily focused on mechanical properties in the as-cast state, with early papers (PMC7514121, 2018) subtracting various elements from HfMoNbTaTiZr to quantify individual influences on strength and ductility, and subsequent work (PMC7514597, 2019) examining partial subsets (3- and 4-element combinations) to assess microstructure and mechanical performance at room temperature. These efforts achieved improved strength–ductility balances but did not address the alloy’s poor oxidation resistance at elevated temperatures, leaving oxygen attack as an unresolved limitation.
decision.unsolved: Despite enhanced high-temperature strength and ductility, degradation by oxygen infiltration (pesting) remains unaddressed for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, restricting practical use above ~800 °C. Existing studies have demonstrated pesting prevention in non-equiatomic variants and related alloys, but no proven method has been applied to this exact equiatomic composition to protect against oxygen while preserving mechanical performance.
decision.lever: Apply a pack-cementation-based silicide surface treatment (e.g., at ~1000 °C for several hours) to form a thin, adherent silicide layer that limits oxygen ingress, with post-treatment microstructure optimized (e.g., controlled thickness ~10–50 µm) to avoid embrittling the sub-surface region.
decision.why: Prior work shows that merely tuning bulk composition or microstructure does not address the root cause of poor oxidation resistance. A targeted surface or interface engineering step allows the bulk alloy to retain its mechanical advantages while establishing a self-protecting silicide scale in air at 800–1000 °C for ≥5 h, based on known approaches in refractory systems. An appropriate lab test would measure mass change and residual mechanical properties after fixed exposures, falsifying the hypothesis if the treated specimens either suffer similar oxidative degradation or lose ductility/strength compared to untreated HfNbTaTiZr.
